To tackle these limitations, there is a growing need to develop more efficient NAS techniques that can effectively explore the extensive search space while also reducing the associated computational costs. To address these challenges, a novel efficient neural architecture search approach called VASNAS is proposed, which employs variable accuracy scheduling to dynamically adjust the accuracy requirements of the candidate models based on their distances from the optimal ones. By doing so, VASNAS expands the effective search space and enables the discovery of more refined models. Moreover, our technique incorporates accuracy regression, which enables the predicted accuracy of the candidate models to be estimated using their architectures and certain key metrics, thereby reducing the need for explicit model evaluation. To validate its effectiveness, our approach underwent extensive evaluation on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets in comparison to the recent efficient NAS techniques, resulting in significant improvements of 0.7% and 1%, respectively, with our technique requiring substantially less computational resources than the competing approaches.

millimeter-wave systems have received little attention in the design of hybrid precoders. To fill this gap, we develop the first integrated design of analog transmit precoders and digital receive combiners for multicasting in mmWave systems, with each device having multiple phases and multiple antennas. By combining semidefinite relaxation, alternating optimization and Cholesky decomposition, we sequentially optimize the digital and analog components at the transmitter and receivers. The proposed method leads to significant performance improvements. Notably, with two receive antennas, we see an average reduction of $ 16.8\% $ in the transmit power needed per message and a rise of $ 44\% $ in the information successfully received. Simulation experiments demonstrate that the designed precoder system functions nearly as well as a fully-digital version even in the presence of difficult transmission conditions.

Unlike conventional Federated Learning, such as Federated Averaging, which increases communication complexity with model size, Federated Distillation reduces communication complexity by utilizing the size of the distillation data set. This study focuses on the correlation of multiple particles in the Hubbard model utilizing the impurity picture, with the aim of analyzing the dynamics of particles in the doped Fermi-Hubbard system and identifying the effects of interactions among particles. We demonstrate the application of the impurity picture to correlate multiple particles and derive a set of correlation functions for one and two particles. The obtained results reveal the dynamics of particles and the impact of interactions among particles, particularly at high densities and in the presence of attractive interactions between particles. These findings are in line with the predictions of previous studies and highlight the significance of considering interactions among particles to understand the observed phenomena. Furthermore, the potential of using the impurity picture to investigate the correlation of multiple particles in quantum simulators is discussed.

addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across all involved domains. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models.

environments using inverse reinforcement learning can face obstacles when experts' demonstrations are marred by extraneous data from their surroundings. This unwanted information is usually eliminated in high-end applications, but in areas like ILRL where data signals are complex and difficult to interpret, filtering this noise is a significant challenge. We've developed a method to address this issue by leveraging the differences between expert and novice performance trajectories. These disparate trajectories are obtained by removing data outliers from both expert and novice suboptimal paths. The outlier removal process relies on a novel distance metric that highlights anomalous data points by comparing trajectory segments. After extracting these anomalies, the paths are refined to eliminate noise and optimize IRL performance, resulting in more accurate reward function and agent trajectory inference. We tested this method on a simulated kitchen navigation problem and found that it outperforms existing IRL models with data cleaning methods, both in terms of reward function accuracy and agent navigation performance.

undergone significant development and growth alongside the expansion of the internet. Since the launch of arXiv in 1991, preprints have increasingly shifted from physical to digital distribution. Preprints enable rapid and low-cost online dissemination of research findings to a broader audience within a matter of days. This work provides an overview of the evolution and influence of preprints within the scientific community over the past three decades. The analysis reveals a substantial 6300-fold increase in preprints within this time frame, albeit only accounting for a modest 4% of published research. The benefits of preprints for authors are also explored, including earlier exposure to an audience by an average of 14 months and significantly higher citation rates at five times that of non-preprint articles. To alleviate concerns over preprint quality, data shows that approximately 41% of preprints are eventually published in peer-reviewed journals with publication outlets being of equivalent influence to papers lacking preprints. The critical role of preprints in communicating emerging research during recent public health crises is also underscored. The quantitative findings presented aim to provide conclusive evidence of the positive impact of preprints on individual researchers and the scientific community, thus enhancing the efficiency of scholarly communication through accelerated and broadened dissemination of research findings facilitated by internet technologies. These metrics can inform policymakers and researchers in strategically employing and responsibly embracing preprints within their respective domains.

While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since the relationships between the variables of the various processes can be quite sophisticated, typically involving multiple steps and interdependent variables, manual calculations are impractical. Given the numerous channels and cross-sections involved, such as those present in top quark pair production or in combinations of boson interactions, the necessary outputs often exceed several thousand variables, rendering manual adjustment impractical. To streamline this process, an intelligent algorithm has been developed that can quickly and effectively reconcile theoretical predictions by modifying matrices based on user-specified requirements, as opposed to traditional approaches where the user would need to manually adjust each output variable individually, a task that is impractical given the complexity of the outputs. This system is then utilized in conjunction with FastNLO SDK, an software that provides an intuitive interface for cutting and normalizing theoretical predictions, as well as preparing them for presentation. Two specific use cases are detailed, the adjustment of parton distribution functions and the cutting of specific kinematic ranges in processes with complex outputs, such as in combinations of boson interactions.

By training a neural network to implicitly generate signed distance function values at any point in three-dimensional space over time, conditioned on a latent code, it is possible to create new and unseen cell shape sequences. Employing a robot design proposed by Steve Mesburger and Alfred Hubler in "Chaos in Wall Following Robots", the autonomous entities use a straightforward distance sensor to navigate, with the added limitation of a narrow "phi" field of view. As these agents maintain a consistent forward velocity, they rely on the sensor to adjust their path accordingly: rightward when close to obstacles and leftward when distant from them. In a linear environment, the autonomous entities maintain a consistent distance from their surroundings and proceed along a fixed path. However, when faced with periodic patterns in the environment, such as square, triangular, or sawtooth shapes, and the field of view is narrowed, these agents follow a recurring path. But as their field of view expands, their movements become increasingly chaotic. A thorough examination, using numerical methods with these shapes, led to the discovery of complex behavior arising from the interaction between the agent's limited field of view and the complexity of the environmental pattern, resulting in a chaotic behavior when the sensor's field of view exceeds a critical value, where within this range the autonomous entities exhibit a recurring pattern while navigating an seemingly random path.

we've found that titanium in barium titanate maintains an unexpected position within the material's crystal structure when it's near by. This finding challenges the common assumption that atoms in a crystal lattice maintain fixed and regular positions. With the newly discovered titanium placement, we've re-created the material's properties from scratch and discovered that this specific arrangement allows for more efficient and stable electric field control. This effect is strongly tied to a special property called the polarizability, which describes how electric fields interact with the material. Yet when these variables have a breakdown in their data due to issues like noise or sampling problems, standard techniques usually fail, until they process the data with a break-down robust alternative. Unfortunately, up to now, there hasn't been a widely used method that can robustly analyze these changes across multiple dimensions while also accounting for any irregular sampling of the data. Moreover, this method should be easily adaptable to various types of analysis. To bridge this gap, we created a breaking down robust method for estimating and forecasting multivariate data based on observations over time or space. By generalizing the concept of (a-t) regression and making use of the \(\alpha\)-optimal robust estimation technique from [1], we developed an easy-to-use equation for analyzing and forecasting multivariate data, even when it's irregularly sampled and potentially noisy. Furthermore, by comparing it with established methods on various practical examples, we demonstrated that our breaking down robust method provides robust and reliable solutions. Ultimately, it allows for a smooth continuation of the data trends even in presence of the data breakdown.

Building on the work of Letamaud and Strahov, we have established that the distribution of the second eigenvalue converges towards a limiting distribution, particularly in scenarios where the Scaler Field Theory (SFT) is applicable. We have also identified a critical threshold p*c, where p*c is equal to 0.648076... (with an associated error of ±0.000031...), beyond which a connected component of size N/((ln(N))^2) exists within the eigenvalue spectrum. Conversely, for p ≤ p*c, the largest eigenvalue is positioned at a distance of O(1) from the real axis. Notably, our results suggest that the two largest eigenvalues become coalesced at a singular point when p approaches p*c from below. Moreover, our eigenvalue distribution data match the predictions of the SFT, particularly in scenarios where the Fractal Spectra Theory (FST) is applicable. We have also established that the distribution of the first two eigenvalues in the limit of large N follows a limiting distribution, with the normalised eigenvalue frequency corresponding to the hydrodynamic function $E^{(2)}_2(x)$, for a given stretch x.

DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to generate continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated, then the genome is partitioned to ensure even distribution among nodes, facilitating efficient computation. Through experimental validation on human and mouse genomes, the proposed algorithm demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods in terms of computational time and accuracy, notably in large, directly repeated sequences, and its scalable architecture allows for seamless integration with high-performance computing systems.

Our study proposes an improved logistic equation with a clearer biological foundation based on cell population dynamics, incorporating discrete and distributed delay terms. The model's global dynamics are fully analyzed and proven to result in all feasible nontrivial solutions converging to the stable positive equilibrium. Utilizing local invariant manifolds, a singular heteroclinic orbit is constructed, linking the unstable zero and stable positive equilibrium. Recent research has developed a point process depth by incorporating a weighted product of two terms - one representing the depth of process magnitude, and the other describing the process as a whole with regards to temporal occurrence. Despite the simplicity of this approach, it lacks a clear connection to point process characteristics, and therefore, it was not possible to determine the influence of specific terms on its effectiveness. To address this, an examination was conducted where the terms contributing to depth are weighted differently, enabling the isolation of their effects, and to evaluate how depth is impacted by the way data are normalized when considering time. By isolating the influence of terms, it was observed that the process characteristic term has a significant impact on depth when data are normalized by time, and that this term's effect is particularly pronounced for processes with isolated active periods. Furthermore, depth was shown to be most sensitive to the process characteristic term for processes with constantly active origins, and that the magnitude term's influence is mostly impacted by 1st order parameters. Ultimately, the isolated analysis and interpretation of terms' effects enabled a clearer understanding of the connection between point process depth and its inherent characteristics.

Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been proven to outperform other approaches in statistical terms. Mathematically, the HDR Lasso is equivalent to an optimization problem with an L1-regularized loss function that utilizes Jaeckel's dispersion function and Wilcoxon scores, making traditional lasso algorithms ineffective due to nondifferentiability. Building on the adaptive sieving strategy from the Exclusive Lasso problem, we introduce a novel HDR Lasso solution that takes full advantage of the problem's sparse nature, solving smaller subproblems in each iteration through the proximal point algorithm, which leverages the problem's nonsmooth terms effectively. Our extensive numerical experiments validate the proposed Adaptive-Sieving Proximal Point Algorithm's robustness across various noise types, as well as its high efficiency, particularly for large-dimensional features, when compared to alternative methods.

However, researchers have lately come to recognize that increasingly complex AI models require substantial amounts of energy to train, thereby contributing to the very emissions they are intended to mitigate. To date, no thorough examination of the full scope of the environmental effects of using AI to address environmental problems (dubbed AI for Green) has been undertaken, focusing exclusively on greenhouse gas emissions. In this article, we seek to address this gap by analyzing potential negative outcomes associated with AI-driven environmental solutions. Initially, we will categorize and analyze various types of AI's environmental impacts. Subsequently, we will present established methods for evaluating these impacts, illustrate the application of life cycle assessment in AI services, and provide an evaluation framework to gauge the environmental utility of general AI services. Lastly, we will highlight the limitations of current AI for Green research initiatives.

a binary neutron star merger in August 2017 paved the way for a new era in multimessenger astronomy. Kilonovae, produced by the expelled material from neutron star collisions, present an attractive opportunity for detection due to their brightened infrared emission and proximity to the site of the gravitational wave source. Furthermore, this phenomenon could generate gamma-ray bursts equivalent to SN 1987's brightness. Researchers analyzed a event candidate, GW190425, using the UKIDEX Extremely Wide Field Camera, a near-infrared survey instrument based in Hawaii, between 2-28 days after the merger event. Although they detected nothing significant, their study provides an initial estimate of a kilonova's light curve and sets limits on the amount of material ejected during neutron star collisions. Researchers used a simple model to interpret their survey results, assuming a specific brightness of ejected material and constrained the amount of material and its color temperature. They further discussed the impact of various factors affecting detection, such as observational protocols and ejecta properties.

implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, a generalized global pooling layer for neural networks called UOT-Pooling (UOTP) has been proposed. To implement this UOTP layer, the classic Sinkhorn-scaling algorithm is employed. Furthermore, a new model architecture based on the framework of optimal transport has been designed, where the parameters of the optimal transport problem are adjusted accordingly, and the resulting layer is referred to as the Optimal Transport-Pooling (OT-P) layer. To test the effectiveness of these new layers, a substantial number of datasets were utilized, and experiments were conducted across multiple applications, including multi-instance learning, graph-based recommendation systems, and conventional deep learning. The results obtained from these experiments indicate that the proposed UOTP and OT-P layers outperform other global pooling layers in terms of accuracy.

aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies which, according to the unified theory, should not exhibit systematic differences depending on AGN classification. We used the SDSS catalogue up to a redshift of 0.2, and the Galaxy Zoo Project catalogue which classifies galaxies into two broad Hubble types, and classified AGNs using emission line diagnostics. Our findings reveal that elliptical galaxies have a significantly higher fraction of Type 1 Seyfert nuclei compared to other AGN types, and the transition from Seyfert 1 to LINER, Type 2 Seyfert, and composite nuclei corresponds to a rise in spiral host galaxies. These findings contradict the unified model, and suggest that there's a symbiotic relationship between supermassive black holes and galactic bulges. Furthermore, our data indicate that spiral host galaxies with Type 1 Seyfert nuclei predominantly face towards the observer, whereas the distribution of Type 2 Seyfert nuclei orientations aligns with those of star-forming galaxies but does not fully match, and is consistent with a contribution of the galactic disc to the obscuration of the nuclear region. These results are consistent with those of earlier studies, and based on this, we propose an updated version of the unified model, and also provide an alternative explanation for the'starburst-active galactic nucleus' connection.

the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. Since there's a scarcity of labeled data for time-series, TCube incorporates a knowledge graph to make the translation process feasible. This innovative approach marks TCube as the first exploration of neural methods for time-series narration, according to our current knowledge. In our comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that TCube significantly improves the variety of words in the generated stories, while also maintaining correct grammar, by up to 65.38%. Furthermore, an expert review of 21 professionals showed that 76.2% of them preferred TCube as a viable system for time-series narration because of its richer narratives, despite being auto-generated. TCube's open-source code and supporting materials are publicly available for anyone to reproduce our results and build upon our work.

These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $|\ln t|^\gamma$ where $0 < \gamma < 1$. By applying a specific metric on the phase space, we can categorize these equations and examine their coefficients, which have polynomial bounds in x, x-derivatives, and a specific rate of decrease in t. We leverage a Planck function, based on this metric, to split the phase space and define relevant generalized symbol classes. Through the use of a conjugating pseudodifferential operator, which we term the loss operator, we establish an energy estimate and identify a link between the loss of regularity and the phase space metric and singular behavior. Our analysis shows that the solution undergoes a small, yet arbitrary, loss in regularity and exhibits a non-regularizing, time-dependent behavior. Furthermore, we prove that the solution's norm, calculated using a Sobolev norm and generalized symbol classes, remains within a bounded interval for all positive t.

Boost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. Users are generally unable to discern how individual characteristics, or sets of characteristics, influence these models as their values change. In order to improve this understanding, a method called Disentangled Attribution Curves has been introduced to offer more transparent explanations for tree ensemble models through detailed (multi-dimensional) curves depicting feature importance at different variable values. By using this new approach, it is possible to boost the accuracy of regression models and maintain clarity in how their predictions are made, as demonstrated on real-world data and further validated in simulation studies where it was found to surpass alternative methods in recovering predictive models. Finally, a practical analysis using bike-sharing data highlights the utility of DAC in uncovering valuable new insights.

We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first establish a framework for defining linear classification models within curved, high-dimensional spaces that generalize traditional vector-based classification.
Next, we demonstrate that, regardless of the geometry of the space, linear classification models are capable of accurately predicting any $d+1$ data points.
We've then formalized the application of these models in complex product space structures and have developed new types of classifiers for such environments, providing solid theoretical backing for their effectiveness.
Moreover, our analysis reveals that these classifiers can learn complex relationships within high-dimensional data, but we've established that they can only handle at least $d+1$ data points. To substantiate these claims, we tested our methods on various data sets, including synthesized data, image information, and data from single-cell RNA sequencing experiments, observing an approximately $15\%$ average performance gain when applied to low-dimensional representations of the latter data type compared to traditional Euclidean-based classification approaches.

MA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than those generally obtained from binary formation simulations, which were around $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$. In response to these disparities, researchers carried out numerical simulations of core accretion and merger events in equal-mass binary systems to analyze how these processes influence proto-stellar mass estimates. In scenarios where a low-mass envelope surrounds a proto-star after $10^5$ years, a more massive companion may provoke thermal emission from the envelope, falsely indicating a higher mass proto-star estimate. In cases where a proto-star dominates the emission, its estimated mass may be influenced by whether or not the companion has cooled down or is emitting thermal radiation. These phenomena highlight the complexity of core accretion and binary merger events, while also noting that a number of unknown factors such as grain settlement and radiation pressure may play even more critical roles in determining proto-stellar mass estimates.

An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework leveraging social media. It addresses spatial resolution ambiguity through a quad-tree based method that segmentates regions based on data density, and uses statistical analysis incorporating the Poisson distribution to highlight anomalies in post density. Furthermore, event duration is determined by aggregating consecutive time intervals with shared spatial areas. An added filter is incorporated to remove spam, false, or inaccurate events. The framework incorporates entity-based analysis to evaluate event credibility and reliability. Evaluation is performed using multiple datasets for distinct cities, including Melbourne, London, Paris, and New York, and is benchmarked against existing approaches employing fixed spatial divisions and clustering algorithms. Assessment of recall and precision are manually computed, and a novel metric called strength index is proposed to evaluate event accuracy.

Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence loss, outperform the widely used cross-entropy loss, especially under constraints such as data scarcity and memory limitations. The effectiveness of these underappreciated loss functions is attributed to their ability to discourage overconfident predictions, a desirable trait in uncertain environments. Furthermore, the underappreciated loss functions exhibit improved generalization capabilities, particularly when subjected to data augmentation, as they prevent overfitting by limiting prediction confidence.

This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but an actual material realization has eluded scientists. Recent studies on TmSe$_{1-x}$Cl$_{x}$ made significant progress, but the presence of disorder due to chlorine substitution made it difficult to determine if an true excitonic gap existed. To address this question, our team performed an in-depth investigation of TmSe using advanced spectroscopic techniques and computational tools. Our data reveal a distinct indication of an excitonic gap at the Fermi level in TmSe at temperatures between 2 and 10 K, exhibiting notable diversity. This finding is supported by our computational results, which show that the observed features can't be replicated using standard band structure models, but can be accurately modeled as a result of an excitonic gap. Our research presents substantial evidence that TmSe is the long-awaited material that exhibits an excitonic gap under ordinary conditions.

causal parameter that can be estimated by treating observational data as though it were from a randomized trial, assuming key conditions, including the absence of confounding, can be met. When this ATE estimate is subject to uncertainty, a confidence interval can be derived using the distribution of an ATE estimator - specifically the Difference-in-Means estimator in the context of the ATE. This study explores the properties of Difference-in-Means confidence intervals under specific data structures known as Simple Random Samples and Propensity Score Matching. Although Difference-in-Means intervals are often hailed as providing 'automatic' confidence intervals for the ATE, this work reveals that they fail to produce valid results when data is not randomly sampled and instead yields empty intervals that fail to accurately capture uncertainty. Propensity Score Matching, when unsuccessful in eliminating confounding, also results in empty intervals, with fates similar to Difference-in-Means under Simple Random Samples. However, when Propensity Score Matching can be deemed successful in eliminating confounding, it produces valid intervals. To facilitate accurate estimation of the ATE, this research recommends alternative methods that account for potential confounding using data augmentation, specifically the Bayesian version of the ATE estimator and the Bayesian bootstrap, both of which can produce valid results when data is not randomly sampled. The findings detailed herein were verified through numerical analysis and replicated with real-world data exemplars. The associated software code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jknowlesphd/difference-in-means-confidence

The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method diminishes in cases where strong nonlinearity affects its accuracy. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn comprehensive models, differentiating between linear and nonlinear interactions; however, it is limited in its application to lower dimensional systems. We introduce a new approach, called dynamic localization of nonlinearity, that combines the dynamic mode decomposition technique with a linear dimensionality reduction method and a synthetic grid to analyze the local dynamics of a system. This approach allows for the identification of genuine modes, a comprehensive model structure, and a measure of error that corresponds to the level of nonlinearity present. We test this method using diverse systems of data and observe its successful application to data from fluid dynamics, chemical reactions, and atmospheric phenomena.

we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and to Kerr black holes.

The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also exists in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending solely on dissipation properties; (ii) It undergoes a type of supercritical bifurcation; and (iii) It's minimally affected by factors like the fracture energy associated with a certain dissipation time. These results support the idea that these intrinsic scales play a universal role in understanding and modeling the oscillatory instability observed in 2D fracture experiments.

graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. It's proposed that remote epitaxy could account for observations of 30 degree rotations in other systems, and potentially also applies in cases of epitaxial pairing leading to domain formations.

However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the presence of noisy labels during training.  To address these challenges, we introduce ANNA, an automatic method that uses abnormal detection algorithms based on cardiac auscultation sounds with background noise present.  The approach involves learning from noisy lamp posts, as it were, by using a latent representation of the audio signals through contrastive learning, thereby isolating the cardiac signals from the background noise.  The background noise is encoded as pseudo-positive examples in contrastive learning, facilitating the learning of robust features.  The method also uses pseudo-labels to improve training, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of the cardiac auscultation sound classifier.  The performance of ANNA was evaluated on large datasets consisting of cardiac auscultation sounds with background noise, and compared with existing state-of-the-art methods.  The results revealed that ANNA yielded overall performance scores of 0.9171 and 0.9173 in terms of precision and recall, respectively, far surpassing prior methods.

Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup with multiple interference paths was used to demonstrate that these systems break electron-hole symmetry. As a result, an electron charge current can be directed from hot to cold or vice versa, and an accompanying heat current is also predicted. These findings can be attributed to a simple and logical physical interpretation. Furthermore, heat rectification can be achieved by combining two quantum Hall systems with different filling factors, and this effect can be enhanced through the design of a specific interference pattern.

A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum model for identifying patterns in datasets by leveraging quantum machines learning capabilities. Utilizing the embbedding of discrete Hebrew alphabet in qubits, we train a quantum model to recognize patterns in datasets from 6 to 32 items. Our results demonstrate that large quantum machines can outperform smaller ones in terms of accuracy, yet the latter possesses significant advantages in runtime. In particular, for a 16-item dataset, a 5-qubit model attains similar accuracy to its 11-qubit counterpart, while reducing the runtime by a substantial margin. This showcases the potential of smaller quantum machines to efficiently handle datasets of practical size for real-world applications.

Building on existing work in random graphs and sparsest paths, this study introduces the concept of shortest paths in random networks with multiple edges. By simulating origin-destination demand and network disruptions through edge deletions, this research quantifies the probability that the shortest path between two points becomes inaccessible. Through numerical analysis and the example of a small network, this study reveals that even in highly connected random networks with an average degree of $20$, the probability of path disruption can be significant. Conversely, in sparse networks with an average degree of $0.5$, the probability of path disruption is indistinguishable from its theoretical minimum in highly connected networks. Moreover, this study proposes an efficient algorithm to compute the shortest paths in random networks and study the distribution of their lengths, revealing both theoretical and numerical evidence of a concentration phenomenon around the mean. Finally, this research examines the effect of multiplying or adding weights to estimate the probability of path disruption and shows that even with weak weighting factors, the shortest path length distribution converges to its mean with high precision.

SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions such as social distancing measures to curb the virus spread and maintain the healthcare system functionality. With the isolation of communities, access to reliable information has become restricted. Consequently, the health minister in South Africa updates the public every day on COVID-19 infections, including affected individuals' demographic and travel details. Meanwhile, the National Institute for Communicable Diseases provides daily updates on testing numbers, case counts, and fatality rates via infographics but often fails to release patients' ages or other critical details. South Africa's health ministry has emerged as the primary source of reliable information on the pandemic, sharing knowledge on transmission protocols, testing processes, and related health issues. This paper will focus on monitoring the government's communication strategy by analyzing the ministry's statements on COVID-19 in a social media forum to discuss their approach. Furthermore, we will compare the government's response to that of New York, a heavily affected US state, to identify best practices in data disclosure and transparency.

To test this hypothesis, we conducted a study using a small dataset containing 460 pairs of COVID-19 negative patients and severe COVID-19 patients from China's Wuhan city and South Korea's Daegu city. During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture object-to-object relationships and a spatial mask decoder that learns the relative positions of objects within a scene. Overall, SABRA leads to a substantial decrease in false positives and improves relationship detection and overall model performance. Notably, it achieves state-of-the-art results on the VisDrone 2012 and KITTI-TOFS datasets.

Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. This is caused by the emission's power law suppression of lower-energy frequencies. To determine the upper limit on the fraction of primordial black holes in dark matter, we used data from the radio observations of Edelstein-Sidor and motivated an equation that connects the black holes' mass function to the radio spectrum's index and excess power. We discovered that the data significantly restricts the fraction of dark matter comprised by these black holes, typically to less than 10% of the excess above the cosmic microwave background. In the most extreme scenario, the fraction is at most 40%. We also identified a potential correlation between the dark matter-induced radio excess and the distribution of gamma-ray sources, Sgr A*'s companion stars, and fast-moving stars near the galactic centre that may be caused by primordial black holes.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Lov\'asz theta function for approximating the Tenerini number. Meanwhile, Fowler obtained a PTAS for specific graph classes using the standard approach but encountered an apparent technical issue.

The main issue with Fowler's method lies in dealing with precise value computations of the search problem's influence function, which makes it impractical. To resolve this, we demonstrate that such precise values can be substituted with an upper bound derived from Pajunes' work without compromising the PTAS guarantee.

PTAS also guarantees the efficiency of a search problem with limited depth, which allows us to derive a search PTAS with an approximately linear search depth on certain graph classes under specific conditions.

Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of UPIO over existing unsupervised parsing models on the WSJ domain of the Penn Treebank bank. Additionally, we found UPOA and UPIO to be effective in processing sentences with errors in syntax and those containing multiple sentences. UPIO was also shown to be versatile and could be applied to improve other parsing models as well as the semantic interpretation of sentences with complex syntax.

rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect them to exhibit a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we used Gaia's latest rotation rate data and mathematical modeling to determine the core rotation rate, which suggests a significantly faster core rotation rate than the outer layers. Additionally, we identified what could be the star's stable eigenmode, which aligns with seismic data, as well as revealed an intriguing pattern of decreasing oscillation period with increasing mode degree at certain angular frequencies.

This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST-DELAY-lin, an enumeration class of problems that can be computed after linear-time preprocessing. The proposed computation model has limited storage and processing capabilities - its registers can store $O(N)$ elements, where $N$ is the input size, and operations take unit time. The success of this foundation will be built upon demonstrating that the newly defined RAM model is equivalent to the traditional one, and then establishing the existence of problems that necessitate linear-time input processing for the given machine model but are computable with linear additional processing capacity. Additionally, the work includes an analysis of the linear-time computability class and its relations with other established classes, including E, P, and CONST-DELAY-lin.

By leveraging the properties of these sequences, the approach is able to identify the optimal subsequence for each user' s request. Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and therefore dominates at higher frequencies. Failing to accurately account for SGWMB could lead to incorrect conclusions, but properly investigating it might enable the detection of supermassive binary black holes. Furthermore, studying SGWMB offers a novel method to identify gravitational wave memory and provides an opportunity to advance our understanding of gravity theory.

A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic words groups, but it overlooks the order of words and their grammatical functions. On the other hand, contextual language models can generate coherent sentences, yet their ability to capture semantic relationships is limited. To address this, hybrid models that integrate both methods have been experimented with, yielding promising outcomes in specific scenarios. In this research, we introduce Context-Aware Language Models that incorporate semantic relationships, combining word order analysis, to successfully address the word prediction challenge. Our approach starts with building a contextual graph representation for words in a sentence by leveraging WordNet, defining contextual graphs for words through connections in both semantic networks and sentence context, and selecting high-relevance words in semantic networks to create contextual graphs. We have developed an automatic system that constructs contextual graphs for words in a sentence from the corpus of English texts in Wikipedia. We have tested our method in the word prediction challenge with both a Wikipedia and WordNet-based corpus, achieving an accuracy of 57.95% with a contextual graph size of 10 nodes and 5 nodes in the generated contextual graph for words.

Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds under conditions typically seen in galaxy clusters. Our results indicate that filamentary segments of these clouds quickly cool and separate from the surrounding hot intracluster medium before ultimately fragmenting and creating numerous smaller clumps. generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then clustered into acoustic units using the K-means algorithm. To generate speech from text without transcription, the starting point is to locate the target units in the training data through a search operation. The text-to-speech synthesis process is completed using an exclusive-or based synthesis method. The results show that the proposed system with transient and steady-state units can produce high-quality speech with lower error rates than the conventional CV units.

motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot.

manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.

This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to refine the performance limits of one-shot and multi-copy probabilistic resource distillation protocols.
Concurrently, we introduced a comprehensive technique for calculating achievable probabilities in resource transformations through a series of convex optimisation problems.
This approach enabled us to precisely assess the trade-offs between probabilities and errors in the distillation of maximally resource-rich states.
Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our methods in the analysis of quantum entanglement distillation.

The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance.

known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-proof" and "sometimes-proof," which have received significant research attention. Past studies on the "always-proof" type have primarily involved perfect correlations from bipartite states, whereas the "sometimes-proof" type has been explored using a variety of methods, including the construction of unextendable sets of correlations. Notably, it remains uncertain if the "always-proof" type can be achieved using perfect correlations from n-partite states. This study showcases the "always-proof" type achieved through perfect correlations from tripartite states, thereby resolving this uncertainty, and further highlights its similarity to past constructions using bipartite states. Additionally, the study presents a method of translating certain tripartite unextendable sets of correlations into Bell nonlocality "sometimes-proof".

has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not equal to zero, and a generalised equality relation applicable to all quantities.

In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Our work reveals that if a type $T$ can transform sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers and if forkability of $T$ and $T(e_1...e_n)$ decreases infinitely with every added sequence vector $e_i$, then the sequence's vector space is linearly independent only when the dimension is infinite. We also use this result as a model to demonstrate that if a system has no atomic model $M$ such that $T$ is orthogonal to $M$, then the sequence's vector space is linearly independent only when the dimension is infinite.

conjecture in black hole physics involves complex analysis driven by the thermodynamics of black holes. We've explored the thermodynamics of a spherically symmetric black hole field system, incorporating scalar field and a massless scalar field, to examine the dynamics of thermodynamic quantities such as entropy, temperature, and pressure. Using the Feferman-Graham expansion for the black hole metric and a conformal version of the Dirac gauge invariant quantization method for the coupled field system, we've analyzed how thermodynamic parameters behave during the black hole's evolution. Furthermore, we've computed an entropy associated with the U(1) current, consistent with the area law, and investigated the near-horizon region's geometric properties. Additionally, we've discussed the black hole's final state following the collapse of a scalar field, accompanied by the formation of a conformal black hole. Lastly, addressing the cosmic censorship conjecture, we've computed the mass loss due to the emission of two types of waves: the Dirac gauge invariant and the massless wave, which provides insight into the Cajias-Zannetti-Barnich crash criterion, potentially shedding light on the conjecture.

focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G's set actions. We then explore Schreier growth gaps for solvable groups. If G is metabelian and finitely presented or torsion-free, but not virtually abelian, it possesses a Schreier growth gap of n^2. If metabelian G has a Krull dimension of k, it will have a Schreier growth gap of n^k, such as the Schreier growth gap n^d for the wreath product C_p ∋¬ ℤ^d and n^(d+1) for ℤ ∋¬ ℤ^d. For solvable groups of finite Prüfer rank, a Schreier growth gap of exp(n) applies unless they are virtually nilpotent, a criterion which also applies to solvable groups linear over ℚ. Lastly, a wide range of torsion-free solvable groups have a Schreier growth gap of n^2, a group type that also includes those linear over ℚ.

The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns.

(ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass using ML, we highlight the limitations of purely data-driven approaches to physics. Despite being able to fit the measurement data accurately, the resulting models do not accurately describe the universal behavior governed by the law of gravity, cannot distinguish between noise and relevant discrepancies, and are unable to detect the impact of larger systematic errors. Furthermore, they may incorrectly infer universal constants and even derive conflicting gravitation equations based on measurements that apparently follow the law of gravity. To successfully infer a universal physical law, it is crucial to have high-quality, precise, and detailed numerical data, as well as a solid understanding of potential systematics and the sources of measurement uncertainty, which can be tailored to fit various object sizes and masses.

Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias towards handling OoD scenarios.

This robust feature set is generated using the Rich Feature Construction (RFC) algorithm, also known as Bonsai, which comprises a sequence of iterative training episodes. Using the Bonsai representation, we evaluate several simple model architectures on six benchmark datasets and two sobol sampling scenarios, while fixing the hyperparameters in a designed manner to compare our approach with prior art. Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and local positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent components of a single fluid.
Gravity emerges from the interaction between these random fields and ordinary matter, causing a significant positive pressure near matter sources due to high energy density.
Consequently, the pressure within these sources outweighs the negative dark energy fluctuations, resulting in the outward force that gives rise to the phenomenon we observe as gravity.
The remaining dark energy, comprising about 68% of the total, is thought to be the result of a true vacuum state that has yet to be reached, with the true vacuum state having a significantly lower energy level than the false vacuum state.
It's hypothesized that when the true vacuum state is reached, the dark energy fluctuations will cease, and the remaining dark matter fluctuations will consolidate into a singularity marking the end of the current phase of expansion.
This theory simplifies the fundamental laws of physics, positing that all matter and energy exist as a single fluid with a single pressure characteristic, and predicts that a true vacuum state will eventually be attained.
As a result, the remaining dark matter fluctuations will consolidate into a massive singularity that marks the end of the current phase of expansion.

The algorithm presented in this research determines the most significant implications that can occur within a data set based on support and confidence criteria. A novel algorithmic method has been developed to identify and group implications as unions of partial scenes. High support implications can be described as complete scenes, whereas others are referred to as partial scenes. Implications with low support can be categorized as direct or indirect partial scenes. Direct partial scenes involve implications where one item directly includes another, whereas indirect partial scenes involve implications with multiple items. The association rule analysis method presented in this research allows for the identification of direct and indirect partial scenes using graph representations and union finding algorithms. Experimental results have demonstrated that the method performs optimally on data sets containing direct partial scenes and competes competitively with current methods on data sets containing indirect partial scenes.

By analyzing a model of the map estimation process, it is possible to examine the trade-off between training point density and the accuracy of the resulting map at any given location. Additionally, a novel measure of map accuracy is introduced, and several algorithms are developed to assess the impact of different training strategies on map estimation. It is shown that a UAV can effectively generate a map using a sparse set of training points, and the resulting map can be used to estimate the levels of interference present at unknown locations.

In this study, we explore dust density and temperature changes in a protoplanetary disk that surrounds a star that is one solar mass. We use observations from the Mid-Infrared Mapping Camera on the JCMT and the Herschel Space Observatory to investigate a gas-rich disk around a star that is one solar mass. We discovered a significant dust density gap at a distance of 63 astronomical units from the star and a noticeable reduction in dust temperature at a distance of around 220 astronomical units. We found that the dust temperature across the disk follows a general pattern of decreasing temperature with distance, but only outside of the density gap. By accounting for stellar irradiance and dust properties, we determined that the temperature drops at a rate of 0.68 K au-1 outside of the density gap and 0.36 K au-1 within it. We found that the observed data can be explained by the interaction of a planet with a mass less than 0.7 Jupiter masses that is orbiting the star at a distance of around 220 astronomical units. The planet's gravitational influence is limited to a small radius and does not significantly affect the gas in the disk, which is consistent with observations.

By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real physical structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. These simulations suggested that the observed features could be attributed to an effect known as "spoonbing" where the concentration of stars in the Milky Way's disk concentrates stars into apparent structures.

Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion. Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified form of X's links when the link size of X is O(log |X|). The basis of this algorithm is rooted in Lubotzky, Samuels, and Vishne's groups from 2005 that created the first discovered high dimensional expanders. Our work includes an efficient algorithm for producing covers of betti numbers but unfortunately, our current implementation falls short of efficiently handling the full range of link sizes in X, leaving Y with links of size O(log |X|). To overcome this limitation, our results suggest an innovative approach that may lead to a future development of a betti number estimator for infinite groups.

energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons, which can then interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultra-peripheral collisions occur when high-energy ions surpass the range of the strong force, enabled by virtual photons exchanged between the nuclei, whose numbers directly correlate with nuclear electric charge. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as pressure increased, Mn$_3$Sn shifted from a conventional antiferromagnetic ground state to a helical state, where a required characteristic for the anomalous Hall effect is absent. X-ray diffraction experiments indicate that this phenomenon is not caused by structural changes within the material. The investigation further reveals that when Mn$_3$Sn enters the helical state, its in-plane lattice parameter exhibits unusual temperature-dependent behavior. The discovery of pressure-induced helical state and associated anomalous Hall effect suppression could potentially stimulate the development of innovative antiferromagnetic spintronics applications.

cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Neural Networks with Inverse Depth (DCNN-ID), are developed by adjusting hyperparameters to achieve optimal generalization performance. By substituting network weights with a set of optimal 'inverses' of weights, which are learned alongside their corresponding original weights, DCNN-ID models outperform traditional neural networks and have faster convergence rates during training. Building upon this concept, we introduce a new method based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to efficiently update the inverses of weights in real-time. Experimental evaluations on a range of benchmark datasets, including MNIST and CIFAR-10, demonstrate improved generalization performance and faster training speeds for DCNN-ID models using the ADMM approach compared to standard neural networks.

Jets within the central lead-lead events exhibited a higher yield of low-energy particles, paired with a decrease in high-transverse-momentum particles, roughly transitioning at a point around 3 GeV. This study is the first to demonstrate alterations in parton (dominated by quarks) showers traversing the QGP with a known initial trajectory, also offering a controlled system to examine constraints imposed by the medium on fragmentation functions.

semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the behavior of spin polarization within the prototype ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer, which has an in-plane magnetization orientation. Their investigation reveals that this ferromagnetic bilayer displays a rich pattern of spin texture within its uppermost valence bands, which arises from two unique spin cants resulting from the interplay of ferromagnetic order with both chirality and electrical polarization. One type of cant is a result of layer stacking asymmetry and valence state polarization, resulting in equivalent canting patterns on both layers. Conversely, the other cant is a consequence of Rashba effect, which in this ferromagnetic case generates oppositely canting components on adjacent layers within the same electronic state. Additionally, researchers formulated a set of rules governing spin polarization behavior within magnetic crystals based on their magnetic symmetry properties. Lastly, they found that applying compressive strain could effectively control the shape of spin texture within ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayers by creating valence-band states with spins that can be aligned.

rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this phenomenon emerges in old main-sequence stars, it may lead to the generation of solar-type stars exhibiting two layers of differential rotation, with distinct patterns in their latitudes.

This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and is applied to classification, information retrieval, and other related tasks. A significant drawback of traditional two-fan deep Boltzmann machine models lies in their difficulty to handle complex tasks requiring multiple input sources such as image and text description of landscapes. To address this limitation, we introduce the K-fan dBM model with the capability to process multi-input, multi-output data. This is achieved by extending the model's architecture with K-models where each model comprises X and Y components with the capability to perform free-energy minimization. A fan-out layer then distributes input data to these models, while a fan-in layer combines their representations. Following training, a two-step prediction process takes place with a model selecting the most suitable representation and then performing the final prediction with the selected representation. Our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in image classification, object detection, image captioning, and visual question answering tasks. Moreover, we make a significant contribution by combining visual and language inputs to solve complex tasks.

in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient due to the hidden nature of race conditions, which can evade detection by these tests. The McMini model checker, which is based on DPOR, has been expanded with a mechanism that enables the declaration of novel, fundamental thread operations through C code. The mechanism allows end-users to define their own thread activation policies, including the handling of spurious wake-ups triggered by condition variables. By specifying (i) when operations are allowed, (ii) the order of thread activations, and (iii) the duration of each activation, users can influence the scheduling of threads. Although only a limited set of thread operations is supported by McMini, users can define additional operations, such as reading and writing specific data structures, thereby increasing the versatility of the model checker. The experimental results demonstrate that the novel feature of McMini is effective in verifying practical, real-world multi-threaded programs. Specifically, we have successfully checked the correct usage of standard I/O operations by POSIX, as well as several custom thread operations involving queues and stacks.

It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partition by genetic type. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which counts the number of family groups of size $k$ in the population at time $t$. The frequency spectrum process represents a type of non-Markovian branching process belonging to a class of random-characterized branching processes. This work aims to propose approximation methods that replace this frequency spectrum with simpler quantities and assess the asymptotic error associated with these approximations using central limit theorems. Finally, we apply this model through numerical analysis, focusing particularly on the relationship between one of the proposed approximations and Sabeti's Extended Haplotype Homozygosity measure.
